title: Trump: ‘DEI is dead, equality isn’t’: experts chart path forward amid Trump’s culture war
description_short: Trump: ‘DEI is dead, equality isn’t’: experts chart path forward amid Trump’s culture war
description_medium: ‘DEI is dead, equality isn’t’: experts chart path forward amid Trump’s culture war. Two law professors outline strategies for equality’s survival in a Trumpian post-DEI era in new book How Equality Wins This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: Donald Trump’s attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion programs have helped drive companies and public institutions to retreat from DEI language and initiatives. In How Equality Wins: A New Vision for an Inclusive America, NYU law professors Kenji Yoshino and David Glasgow argue that equality work can continue through approaches designed to reduce bias without assigning opportunities by race or gender. They describe this as “lifting” versus “levelling”: the example they give is symphony auditions, where screens concealing musicians’ identities coincided with women’s representation rising from 5% in 1970 to 35% by 2016. The authors also propose shifting from identity-based cohorts to inclusive course content and considering how race shaped an applicant’s life, an approach they say remains permissible after the Supreme Court’s affirmative-action ruling. They acknowledge that DEI advocates must address criticism of narrow priorities and divisive terminology. Their book argues the project of equality can survive even as its acronym faces political attacks and legal scrutiny.

title: Trump-aligned candidates surge as some incumbents fall: five key takeaways from US primary elections
description_short: Trump-aligned candidates surge as some incumbents fall: five key takeaways from US primary elections
description_medium: Trump-aligned candidates surge as some incumbents fall: five key takeaways from US primary elections. description_long: The March 2026 primaries offered early signs of how voters were responding to Trump-era politics ahead of the midterms. In Texas, Republican Dan Crenshaw lost his primary to Steve Toth, who was more closely aligned with Trump; Toth received nearly 56% while Crenshaw won 41%. Two other Texas House races remained unsettled: Al Green trailed Christian Menefee in a runoff, while conservative YouTuber Brandon Herrera led Tony Gonzales amid calls for Gonzales to resign over allegations involving an aide. In Arkansas, Democrat Alex Holladay won a state House special election with 57% against Republican Bo Renshaw, though the result did not change Republicans’ legislative majority. North Carolina voters ousted three Democratic lawmakers who had sometimes joined Republicans to override Governor Josh Stein’s vetoes. The roundup presented these contests as clues to voter sentiment and party energy, not a forecast of November results. Several races remained open or close, leaving the wider midterm picture unsettled.

title: Trump Fires VA Secretary David Shulkin via Tweet
description_short: Trump Fires VA Secretary David Shulkin via Tweet
description_medium: On March 28, 2018, Donald Trump announced by tweet that VA Secretary David Shulkin was leaving and nominated White House physician Ronny Jackson as his replacement. Shulkin’s departure followed an inspector general report on government-funded travel. Jackson later withdrew after senators raised concerns and misconduct allegations surfaced.
description_long: On March 28, 2018, President Donald Trump announced on Twitter that Veterans Affairs Secretary David Shulkin was leaving his post and that White House physician Ronny Jackson would be nominated as his replacement. Shulkin’s departure followed internal efforts to push him out and an inspector general report concerning his use of government funds for travel. Shulkin later described his removal as the work of political ideologues seeking to privatize the VA; that is his account of the dispute, not an independently established motive. Jackson’s nomination did not proceed: it collapsed after senators raised concerns about his suitability, and he withdrew amid allegations of misconduct. The episode illustrates both the abruptness of Trump’s personnel announcement and the Senate’s role in reviewing a nominee. The supplied reporting supports those immediate facts, but does not establish that privatization caused Shulkin’s firing or that the department’s policies changed as a result. title: EPA Proposes Repealing All Greenhouse Gas Rules for Power Plants, Weakening Mercury Limits
description_short: EPA Proposes Repealing All Greenhouse Gas Rules for Power Plants, Weakening Mercury Limits
description_medium: On June 11, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin proposed repealing power-plant greenhouse-gas standards and weakening mercury and air-toxics limits. EPA projected $19 billion in industry savings over 20 years; environmental groups warned of increased toxic exposure and climate pollution. The changes were proposals, not finalized rules.
description_long: On June 11, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced proposals to repeal greenhouse-gas limits for fossil-fuel power plants and weaken the 2024 Mercury and Air Toxics Standards. The administration said the changes would reduce regulatory costs for the power sector by $19 billion over two decades. Zeldin attacked climate action as a “cult,” while EPA advanced a legal argument that it must first determine whether power-plant greenhouse-gas emissions significantly contribute to dangerous air pollution before regulating them. Environmental groups warned that weaker controls could leave more people exposed to mercury, arsenic and lead and increase climate pollution. Those health and climate effects were forecasts made in response to proposed rule changes, not measured outcomes. The announcement opened a regulatory process; it did not immediately repeal the existing standards. The dispute set the administration’s cost and legal arguments against opponents’ concerns about pollution and public health. The proposals targeted rules associated with coal and other fossil-fuel generation, sectors where the standards can affect plant operation and retirement decisions.

description_long: J.D. Vance told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins that he was “extremely skeptical” Mike Pence’s life had been in danger during the January 6 attack on the Capitol. title: Trump Campaign & RNC sue Pennsylvania to stop all mail-in voting
description_short: Trump Campaign & RNC sue Pennsylvania to stop all mail-in voting
description_medium: The Trump campaign and Republican National Committee sued Pennsylvania officials in 2020 to block mail-in voting. A federal judge dismissed the case, calling the campaign’s fraud claims speculative after it declined to provide evidence of actual fraud. The ruling did not establish the allegations behind the lawsuit.
description_long: In 2020, the Trump campaign and Republican National Committee sued Pennsylvania election officials in an effort to stop the state from using mail-in ballots. The campaign argued that the system weakened in-person voting safeguards and increased the risk of fraud. A federal judge later dismissed the case, describing the campaign’s fraud claims as speculative and saying the plaintiffs had not shown that fraud was “certainly impending.” The judge had asked the campaign to provide evidence of actual fraud, but it declined, arguing that it did not need to do so to prevail. The case therefore ended without establishing the fraud allegation used to support the challenge. The lawsuit was part of a broader effort to contest voting rules before the 2020 election and sought to limit a method of voting available to Pennsylvanians. The court’s ruling distinguished the campaign’s claims from evidence sufficient to justify blocking mail-in voting.

description_long: In Red Mafiya, his 2000 investigation of Russian organized crime, journalist Robert I. He argued that this transnational influence could threaten democratic institutions. Friedman had spent years reporting on Russian organized crime, and the book became a major account of its growth and connections. His warning addressed how illicit networks might exploit legitimate commerce and political relationships; it was not a claim that every institution in the regions named had been captured. The work belongs to the broader history of reporting on post-Soviet criminal organizations and their international activity. Friedman died in 2002.
